html:
Surah Ar-Raḥmān (The Most Merciful) is the 55th surah of the Qur’an — seventy-eight verses, mostly classified as Makkī by Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī, with a minority Madanī opinion for one or two passages. It is the only surah that opens with a single divine name — Ar-Raḥmān — standing alone as its first verse. That opening is itself the thesis: everything that follows is a catalogue of what the All-Merciful has given, taught, built, measured, suspended, split, and promised. The surah is distinguished by its refrain “Then which of your Lord’s favours will you deny?” (fa-bi-ayyi ālā’i Rabbikumā tukadhdhibān), repeated thirty-one times, interleaved between every category of blessing: the stars that make navigation possible, the balance that makes justice possible, the two seas that do not transgress each other, the paired paradises for the righteous. Ibn Kathīr frames the whole surah as Allah’s direct address to the two weighty creations — jinn and mankind — holding each one accountable for the same mercies.

The best-known virtue narration for Ar-Raḥmān is the Prophet’s ﷺ reported saying: “Everything has a bride, and the bride of the Qur’an is Surah Ar-Raḥmān.” This is recorded in al-Bayhaqī’s Shuʿab al-Īmān 2496 and in Mishkāt al-Maṣābīḥ 2178, narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. The chain contains weaknesses — al-Albānī graded it daʿīf in Daʿīf al-Jāmiʿ 4647, and al-Bayhaqī himself noted the chain is not strong. A separate stronger-looking chain was called ḥasan by some later muḥaddithūn, which is why the saying has circulated widely in works like al-Nawawī’s al-Tibyān and al-Suyūṭī’s al-Durr al-Manthūr. The honest position is to present it as weak but widely narrated: do not quote it as a hadith of the Prophet without the grading, but do not pretend the tradition does not exist. The authentic baseline for the surah’s virtue is the same as for any surah — Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2910 (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ): ten rewards for every letter of the Qur’an. Reciting Ar-Raḥmān is virtuous because reciting Qur’an is virtuous; no special-case bonus is needed to justify making it a weekly companion.

What is firmly established is the Prophet’s practice of reciting Ar-Raḥmān publicly to the jinn. Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 3291 (ḥasan gharīb per Tirmidhī, strengthened by al-Albānī in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Jāmiʿ 4934) records Jābir ibn ʿAbdillāh: “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out to his Companions and recited Surah Ar-Raḥmān to them from beginning to end, and they were silent. He said: ‘I recited it to the jinn on the Night of the Jinn, and their response was better than yours. Every time I came to the saying “Then which of your Lord’s favours will you deny?” they would say: “None of Your favours, our Lord, do we deny — all praise is to You.”’” This gives the refrain its liturgical weight. Classical reciters pause after each repetition precisely to leave space for the listener to repeat the jinn’s answer — lā bi-shay’in min niʿamika Rabbanā nukadhdhib fa-laka al-ḥamd — turning the surah into a responsive confession.

Ibn Kathīr’s structural reading divides the surah into four waves of blessing, each sealed by the refrain. First (verses 1-16): cosmic mercies — the teaching of the Qur’an, the creation of the human, the orbits of sun and moon, the submission of plants and trees, the raising of the sky and setting of the balance (mīzān), and the measured creation of jinn from smokeless fire and man from clay. Second (vv. 17-30): sustaining mercies — the two easts and two wests, the two seas that meet without mixing (an image classical mufassirūn connected to the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mandeb, modern commentators to the halocline), and the pearls and coral that come from them. Third (vv. 31-45): eschatological warning — the Day when neither jinn nor man will escape the courts of Allah, the two torments described in detail, the melting of the sky to crimson rose. Finally (vv. 46-77): the paired paradises — two Gardens for those who feared standing before their Lord, with running springs, pairs of every fruit, companions untouched before, built with their own pillars and shade. The refrain binds these four movements into a single argument: every mercy you accept is evidence you cannot afford to deny the Giver. That, more than any virtue narration, is why the Ṣaḥābah wept at this surah and why reciting it on a Friday night with family — some scholars, including al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, recommended this — is a long-standing practice built on the authentic recitation reward alone.
